answer: NOT FOUND

The RBI requires a commercial bank to ensure adherence to the provisions of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 and the rules made thereunder, and to comply meticulously with any instructions or communications issued by the RBI based on advice from the Ministry of Home Affairs. [S1]
A commercial bank must review its money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment at least annually. [S1]

The bank must temporarily cease operations in the account until the customer submits the PAN or equivalent e‑document or Form No. 60, after giving the customer an accessible notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard. [S1]

A commercial bank must monitor the at‑par cheque facility it offers to co‑operative banks and review the arrangements to assess credit and reputational risks arising therefrom, and it must retain the right to verify the co‑operative bank’s records for compliance with KYC and AML instructions. [S4]
For a remittance of ₹50,000 or more, a commercial bank must fund the demand draft, transfer, or traveller’s cheque by debiting the customer’s account or against cheques, and not by cash payment. [S1]
A commercial bank should identify such countries by referring to the FATF Statements circulated by the RBI from time to time and by consulting publicly available information. [S1]

Under the general restriction, a commercial bank may collect an account payee cheque only for the payee constituent of the account.  
[ S1 ]

The commercial bank must undertake countermeasures when called upon to do so by any international or intergovernmental organisation of which India is a member and which is accepted by the Central Government. [S2]

The RBI’s KYC directions are intended to supplement, not replace, other legal and regulatory obligations.  
Explanation 1 in the Commercial Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures states that “These disclosures are intended only to supplement and not to replace disclosure requirements under other laws, regulations, or accounting and financial reporting standards.” [S3]
Yes. A commercial bank may use V‑CIP to carry out customer due‑diligence (CDD) when onboarding new individual customers and when onboarding the beneficial owners (BOs) of legal‑entity customers【S1】.

After onboarding, a commercial bank must periodically update its customers’ KYC by obtaining a self‑declaration when no change has occurred, ensuring the beneficial ownership information is accurate and up‑to‑date, and verifying that the customer’s KYC documents meet current CDD standards (or re‑doing the full KYC if they do not or have expired) and confirming PAN details from the issuing authority’s database. If any KYC information changes, the bank must carry out a KYC process equivalent to onboarding a new customer. [S1]

No, a commercial bank is not required to perform customer due diligence on every member of an SHG when opening its savings account. The due diligence of all the SHG’s office bearers is sufficient. [S1]

Under the RBI KYC Directions, a commercial bank must adopt a risk‑based approach and categorize its customers into **low, medium, and high‑risk** categories based on its assessment and risk perception. [S1]
Under the RBI’s KYC Directions, a commercial bank must review the risk categorisation of its customer accounts at least once every six months. [S1]

Under the financial education provision, a commercial bank must disclose full‑fledged information on its products and their implications to customers so that they can make an informed judgment about their choice of products. [S1]

A bank must have a transparent, non‑discretionary and non‑discriminatory policy governing the renewal of overdue term deposits, and it must notify the customer of the renewal terms—including the interest rate—at the time the deposit is accepted. [S1]

Yes.  With the issuance of these Directions, all existing RBI Directions, instructions and guidelines that pertain to Responsible Business Conduct for commercial banks are repealed and thus replaced by the new 2025 Directions [S4].

Commercial banks must provide all printed material used by retail customers—including account opening forms, pay‑in slips, passbooks, etc.—in trilingual form: English, Hindi, and the concerned regional language. [S1]

A bank must put in place the necessary infrastructure and facilities and adopt appropriate security measures at every branch where it sanctions loans against gold and/or silver collateral, and it must ensure that such collateral is handled only within its own branches and only by its employees. [S1]
The bank must pay ₹5,000 for each day of delay in settling claims related to safe deposit lockers or articles in safe custody of deceased customers. [S1]
The bank should periodically organise an Exporters’ Meet, and it should be held at centres with a concentration of exporters. [S1]

A commercial bank’s policy must set out the full auction framework, including (i) the trigger event for auction and the timeline for serving an auction notice to the borrower, (ii) the mode of auction, (iii) the notice period allowed to the borrower or legal heir to settle the loan before auction, and (iv) the empanelment of auctioneers [S1]. It must also prescribe the reserve price to be declared at auction – not less than 90 % of the collateral’s current value, or 85 % if the auction fails twice [S3].

Yes – a bank may provide additional facilities beyond the minimum set out in paragraph 86, and it may charge for them or offer them free, provided the offer is non‑discretionary, non‑discriminatory and transparently disclosed to the customer, and no minimum balance is required [S1]. The minimum facilities themselves are those listed in paragraph 86 [S2].
The bank must undertake at least an annual review of accounts that have had no customer‑induced transactions for more than a year. [S1]

Warnings can be posted in the bank branches – for example in the customer lobby or at the “May I Help You” counter – and can also be displayed at ATMs or Business Correspondent Points to reach a wider audience. This approach follows the guidance that such messages should be visible in branches and other high‑traffic locations, and that publicity against dubious schemes should be placed in the branches. [S1] [S2] [S3]
Yes. A commercial bank is responsible for the actions of its recovery agents, and must ensure they strictly adhere to the bank’s instructions while recovering dues. [S2]
The “Enquiry” or “May I Help You” counter must be situated near the entry point of the banking hall, and it is required at all branches except very small ones. [S1]
The prescribed post‑shipment interest rate ceases to accrue from the date the foreign‑currency amount is credited to the bank’s Nostro account. [S1]
A commercial bank must undertake special drives periodically to find out the whereabouts of the customers, their nominees or legal heirs in respect of inoperative accounts or unclaimed deposits. [S1]

A commercial bank must conduct regular audits of its outsourced service providers (including subcontractors) with regard to the services it outsources. These audits may be carried out by the bank’s internal or external auditors appointed to act on its behalf, and should assess the provider’s performance, risk‑management practices and compliance with laws and regulations. [S1] [S3]

The bank should select a group entity based on objective reasons that are similar to the selection of a third‑party, and it must appropriately deal with any conflicts of interest that such an outsourcing arrangement may entail. [S1]

The bank (or NBFC) bears responsibility for the conduct of Direct Sales Agents and recovery agents engaged through a service provider, as it must be accountable for their actions and retain ultimate control over the outsourced activity.  
[S1] [S2]

No – a commercial bank must not engage a non‑group service provider that is owned or controlled by any director, key managerial personnel, the approver of the outsourcing arrangement, or their relatives, unless an exception is granted by the Board or a Committee of the Board with appropriate disclosure, oversight and monitoring. [S1]

Sufficient compliance is achieved if the bank ensures clear separation and isolation of its own and its customers’ data, so that only personnel authorized by the bank can access that data in a multi‑tenant environment. [S1]

Yes.  The RBI’s guidelines state that outsourcing arrangements shall not affect the rights of customers, including the ability to obtain redressal under relevant laws [S1] [S2].  Moreover, a bank must maintain a robust grievance‑redressal mechanism and retain responsibility for customers’ grievances related to outsourced services [S3] [S5].

The outsourcing agreement must give the bank the right to conduct audits on the service provider, either by its internal or external auditors or by agents appointed to act on its behalf, and to obtain copies of any audit or review reports and findings made on the service provider in conjunction with the services performed for the bank. The agreement should also allow the bank to conduct such audits on a regular basis. [S2] [S3]

Yes – a commercial bank may outsource any IT service to an entity within its own business group or conglomerate, provided that the arrangement is backed by a board‑approved policy and appropriate SLAs/agreements with its group entities are in place [S1].

Yes – a commercial bank may adopt a pooled (shared) audit with other regulated entities when they all use the same third‑party IT service provider.  The bank must, however, ensure that the audit requirements related to its contract with the provider are met effectively【S1】.

Commercial banks must evaluate a service provider’s technology, infrastructure, data‑backup and disaster‑recovery arrangements, conflict‑of‑interest issues, data‑segregation capability, regulatory and legal compliance, cyber‑security risk assessment, and the controls, assurance and contractual arrangements that safeguard data protection and confidentiality, while also ensuring the provider can serve all customers and enforce contractual rights [S1]. In addition, due‑diligence should cover qualitative, quantitative, financial, operational, legal and reputational factors, concentration risk, past experience, financial soundness, compliance, complaints, litigation, employee/sub‑contractor vetting, security and internal controls, audit coverage, reporting, monitoring, business continuity, and external political/economic/legal factors, and the outsourcing agreement must include provisions on subcontractors, data access, material adverse events, IT Act compliance, SLAs, and data storage in India [S3][S4].

A commercial bank must keep an inventory of all IT services it outsources to service providers, including key entities involved in their supply chains. The bank should also map its dependency on these third parties and periodically evaluate the information received from the providers. [S2]

A commercial bank must consider the availability of alternative service providers or the possibility of bringing the outsourced activity back in‑house in an emergency, and the costs, time and resources that would be involved in doing so. [S1]

The Board, or a Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated, is responsible for putting in place a framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements at a commercial bank. This includes approving the framework and setting appropriate approval authorities. [S1] [S5]

Yes – the RBI outsourcing requirements apply to subcontracted activities. The bank must obtain prior approval or consent before the service provider engages any subcontractor, review the subcontracting arrangement, and ensure it complies with the Directions set out in Chapter III of the RBI guidelines. [S3]

Commercial banks are prohibited from outsourcing core management functions such as Internal Audit, the compliance function, and decision‑making functions that include determining compliance with KYC norms for opening deposit accounts, giving sanction for loans (including retail loans), and managing the investment portfolio [S2].

A bank must have a risk‑management framework that covers identification, measurement, mitigation, management, and reporting of risks associated with IT outsourcing arrangements [S1]. It must also establish a management structure to monitor and control outsourced services, maintain a central database of all outsourcing arrangements, and ensure that outsourcing agreements contain provisions for monitoring and control [S3][S2][S4].

Commercial banks that issue credit cards and debit cards are subject to the RBI (Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025. These directions govern the conduct of credit‑card business and the issuance of debit cards by such banks, including the record‑keeping requirements for card‑issuers and the application of the directions to loans offered on credit and debit cards. [S4] [S3]

A commercial bank must train its call‑centre staff adequately so they can competently handle and, if necessary, escape a complaint. The grievance‑redressal process must provide for automatic escalation of unresolved complaints from the call centre to higher authorities, and the bank must acknowledge each complaint with a number or docket for follow‑up, even when received by phone. [S1]
A commercial bank must ensure that the card **explicitly indicates it has been issued under a co‑branding arrangement**. This requirement is stated in the RBI guidance for co‑branded cards. [S1] [S5]

We must avoid any actions that could damage our integrity and reputation and must observe strict customer confidentiality when recovering dues, and we and our agents must adhere to the extant Fair Practices Code for lenders. [S1] [S2]

No, a commercial bank does not need prior approval from the RBI before issuing co‑branded credit cards, debit cards or prepaid cards, as the RBI has stated that prior approval is not necessary for such issuances [S1] and that banks do not need approval to become a co‑branding partner [S2].

The card‑issuer must close the credit card account within **seven working days** from the date it seeks OTP‑based consent if the customer does not respond. This is stipulated in the RBI guidelines for commercial banks【S2】 and reiterated in the same provision for unsolicited cards【S1】.

The requirement to seek explicit consent is triggered when the refund amount exceeds **one percent of the card’s credit limit or ₹5,000, whichever is lower**. This threshold applies even if the bill has already been paid. [S1]

The card‑issuer must explicitly inform the customer that the credit history/repayment record is being supplied to the Credit Information Company under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. [S1]

The bank must ensure that every communication sent by its recovery agents to a credit card holder contains the name, email‑id, telephone number and address of the senior officer of the card‑issuer whom the customer can contact. [S1]
A commercial bank may report a credit card account to a credit information company or levy a late‑payment charge only when the account remains past due for **more than three days**【S2】.

No. A commercial bank may not levy any charge that was not explicitly indicated to the cardholder at the time of issue and without the cardholder’s explicit consent, and there must be no hidden charges when issuing credit cards free of charge. [S1] [S3]

Yes.  A commercial bank may issue a business credit card to an individual for business expenses, as stated in paragraph 15 of the Directions [S1].  Business credit cards are defined as cards issued for business expenses and not for personal use [S4].

A commercial bank must have a well‑documented credit‑card issuance and conduct policy approved by its Board or a delegated committee, in consonance with RBI instructions and posted on its website [S1].  
The policy must cover interest‑rate ceilings and other charges, procedures for reporting default status to a Credit Information Company, co‑branding arrangements, standard operating procedures for discretionary blocking/deactivation/suspension of a card, the time period for completing formalities after blocking a lost card, and a redressal of grievances and compensation framework [S3].  
It must also ensure that cardholders receive a record of transactions immediately after completion and that the terms obligate cardholders to keep the card safe and not record the PIN in an intelligible form [S5][S2].
Commercial banks must ensure that wrong bills are not raised and issued to cardholders. [S1]

As a commercial bank, you may disclose only the customer information that is required for DSAs, DMAs and recovery agents to discharge their duties – i.e., information needed for recovery purposes – and you must not release any personal information that is not required for those purposes. The bank must also ensure that such information is kept confidential and not misused by the service provider. [S1] [S3]

The bank must pay interest at the rate applicable to the amount and the period the deposit actually remained with the bank, rather than the contracted rate, and no interest is paid if the withdrawal occurs before the minimum period specified in paragraph 10(1)【S1】.
The minimum tenor for NRE term deposits is one year, while for NRO term deposits it is seven days【S1】.

A commercial bank must be authorised under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) by the Reserve Bank of India before it can accept rupee deposits from non‑residents under NRE and NRO accounts. [S1]
Yes – a bank may grant its staff and their exclusive associations an extra interest of up to **one per cent per annum** over the scheduled rate. [S1]

A commercial bank must treat a deceased depositor’s NRE term deposit as a domestic rupee term deposit at maturity when the claimants are residents. In that case the maturity proceeds are converted into Indian rupees on the maturity date and interest thereafter is paid at the rate applicable to a domestic term deposit of similar maturity. [S1] [S2]
The bank must apply the interest rate specified in the comprehensive policy on interest rate on deposits, subject to the conditions laid down in paragraph 7 of these Directions. [S2]
If a bank accepts an FCNR(B) term deposit without informing the depositor of the penalty components, the exchange loss arising from a premature withdrawal must be borne by the bank. [S1]

For an FCNR(B) deposit renewed within 14 days of maturity, the interest rate payable is the lower of the rate prevailing on the maturity date or the rate prevailing on the date the depositor requests renewal. [S1]

Yes.  As per the repeal clause in the Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, any action taken or purported to have been taken under the repealed directions continues to be governed by the provisions of those old rules【S1】.

A commercial bank is prohibited from levying a penalty for premature withdrawal of a domestic term deposit when the deposit is terminated due to the depositor’s death, when the deposit is split for the claimants of a deceased depositor or joint account holders without any change in period or aggregate amount, or when depositors of a branch wish to withdraw prematurely because the business is being transferred to another bank [S1][S2][S4].

Yes. A bank may, at its discretion, give its resident Indian retired staff who are senior citizens the benefit of additional interest rates as admissible to senior citizens **over and above** the additional interest payable to them by virtue of being retired members of the bank’s staff. [S1]
The minimum credit balance in a farmer’s composite cash credit account is measured from the 10th to the last day of each calendar month for interest calculation purposes. [S1]

A Board‑approved deposit policy must set the interest rate on deposits and prescribe penalties for premature withdrawal of term deposits, including partial withdrawals, and must separately address penalties for premature withdrawal of NRE term deposits and FCNR(B) term deposits. The policy must also state that the components of the penalty are clearly disclosed to depositors at the time of acceptance. [S4] [S2] [S1] [S3]

Yes – a bank must pay interest at the time of converting a deceased FCNR(B) account into an RFC or resident rupee account even if the deposit has not yet reached the minimum maturity period, and the rate paid cannot exceed the rate payable on savings deposits held under the RFC account scheme [S1].

Commercial banks may fund PCFC using foreign‑currency funds borrowed under Notification No. FEMA.3(R)/2018‑RB and foreign‑currency funds generated through buy‑sell swaps in the domestic forex market, subject to the Aggregate Gap Limit in the Master Direction on Risk Management and Inter‑Bank Dealings. [S3]

The bank must ensure that rupee pre‑shipment credit is granted only to exporters with a good track record, that the credit is backed by an export order and complies with trade practices and approved methods of realisation, and that the exporter produces letters of credit or firm orders within a reasonable period; it must then mark off the PCFC on a first‑in‑first‑out basis and liquidate the credit out of the proceeds of bills drawn for the exported goods. [S1] [S3] [S4]

The maximum exposure a commercial bank can have through Partial Credit Enhancements to bonds issued by a single NBFC or HFC is **1 % of the bank’s capital funds (within the extant single/group borrower exposure limits)**. [S1]

Under the RBI’s Commercial Banks – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025, all corporates and other constituent borrowers whose turnover exceeds the threshold level fixed by the bank’s Board of Directors must disclose an aging schedule of their overdue payables in their periodic returns to the bank. [S1]

The bank must grant export credit to an exporter of good track record who has received a direct remittance from abroad by cheque or draft for an export sale, until the proceeds of that cheque or draft are realised. This is required only after the bank is satisfied that the instrument is against an export order, conforms to the trade practices for the goods in question, and is an approved method of realising export proceeds under the extant rules【S1】.

When a commercial bank introduces a new lending product, it must take into account the customer’s suitability and appropriateness and ensure that borrowers are fully aware of the risks and liabilities associated with the product. [S1]

Before releasing funds for a real‑estate loan, a commercial bank must verify the loan application within a reasonable period and, if additional documents are required, inform the borrower immediately [S2]. It must also verify the genuineness of the documents relating to the title of the mortgaged property at the time of acceptance, obtain market reports on the builder/developer, and sanction loans only for projects undertaken by reputed builders/developers [S1].
The builder/developer/company must disclose in the pamphlets or brochures the name(s) of the bank(s) to which the property is mortgaged. [S1]

Yes. A commercial bank must refrain from entering into lease agreements departmentally with equipment leasing companies and other NBFCs engaged in equipment leasing. This is stated in the RBI directions: “they shall not enter into lease agreements departmentally with such companies as well as other NBFCs engaged in equipment leasing” [S1] and “A bank shall not enter into leasing agreement with another equipment leasing company and other non‑banking finance company engaged in equipment leasing” [S2].

Bills rediscounted ‘with recourse’ in the domestic market should be reflected only if the first bank that discounted the bills is the one reporting them; the bank that subsequently rediscounts the bills must not reckon the amount as export credit. [S1]

A bank must value the collateral using the reference price that corresponds to its purity (caratage). It should take the lower of (1) the average closing price for that specific purity over the preceding 30 days, or (2) the closing price for that purity on the preceding day, as published by the India Bullion and Jewellers Association Ltd. (IBJA) or a SEBI‑regulated commodity exchange【S2】.

A microfinance loan is a collateral‑free loan, irrespective of its end use or mode of application, that is provided to low‑income households whose annual income does not exceed ₹3,00,000, and it must not be linked to a lien on the borrower’s deposit account or backed by hypothecation of any security【S5】.

A commercial bank must capture and maintain a project finance database in an electronic, easily accessible format, including at a minimum the following parameters:  

1. **Debtor Profile** – project/SPV name, PAN, LEI, sponsor names, shareholding details, banking arrangement, sector, and sub‑sector.  
2. **Original Project Profile** – nature of the project, external credit rating, economic life, date of financial closure, original date of commencement of commercial operations, total project cost excluding IDC, IDC, capital structure, debt‑to‑equity ratio, debt‑service coverage ratio, repayment tenor, start date, and frequency.  
3. **Change in DCCO** – date of change, reason, extended DCCO, revised project debt, revised total cost, cost overrun, percentage of increase financed by equity and debt, revised debt‑to‑equity ratio, revised debt‑service coverage ratio, revised repayment tenor, start date, frequency, and external credit rating.  

[S1]
No. A commercial bank is prohibited from granting finance for construction of buildings meant purely for Government or Semi‑Government offices, including Municipal offices, as stated in S1.

We may accept DLG only in the following forms: (1) cash deposited with the bank, (2) a fixed deposit maintained with a scheduled commercial bank with a lien marked in favour of the bank, or (3) a bank guarantee in favour of the bank. [S1]

The regulation defines an **Internet Banking Channel** as a digital banking channel that allows customers to operate their accounts and access services over the internet through web‑browser‑based applications, explicitly excluding mobile applications. In contrast, a **Mobile Banking Channel** is defined as a digital banking channel that enables customers to operate their accounts and access services using mobile applications, unstructured supplementary service data (USSD), and short message service (SMS) [S1].

Yes – the RBI may exempt a commercial bank from any provision of the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025, or grant an extension of time to comply, if it deems it necessary to avoid hardship or for any other just and sufficient reason, subject to conditions it may impose [S1].

Commercial banks must comply with the provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and all other applicable legal requirements when conducting digital banking operations, and the jurisdiction for any legal settlement is within India. [S1]

A bank must obtain prior approval of the Reserve Bank and satisfy the eligibility criteria listed in paragraph 7.1 (implementation of CBS and IPv6, CRAR compliance, minimum paid‑up capital, and adequate financial/technical capability) before launching a transactional banking facility. It should apply for this approval through the Department of Regulation, RBI, using the PRAVAAH portal. [S1]

Yes. A commercial bank must obtain explicit consent from the customer before registering them for digital banking services, and it must clearly inform the customer that SMS/email alerts will be sent to the mobile number/email registered with the bank for all operations, both financial and non‑financial. [S1]
Yes – the RBI may issue clarifications and its interpretation of any provision of the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025 is final and binding on all concerned entities. [S1] [S4]

A commercial bank providing digital banking services must comply with the RBI’s “Guidelines on Outsourcing of Information Technology Services” as set out in the **Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing Directions, 2025**. This requirement applies to any outsourced model for the digital‑banking segment, including DBUs, and is explicitly stated in the digital‑banking authorisation and outsourcing guidance. [S1] [S2]

All banks must have implemented a Core Banking Solution (CBS) and enabled their public‑facing IT infrastructure to handle IPv6 traffic before they can offer a view‑only banking facility on internet or mobile channels【S1】.  Once these technical prerequisites are met, the bank must notify the RBI through the PRAVAAH portal and submit a ‘Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy’ (GAICA) report within thirty days of deciding to launch the facility【S1】.

Commercial banks must put in place comprehensive policy(ies) for all digital banking channels that cover all statutory and regulatory requirements, including the management of liquidity and operational risks in a digital banking scenario. [S1]

Yes.  In addition to the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, banks must also comply with other RBI directions that are listed as applicable to digital banking services – such as the Guidelines on Outsourcing of IT Services, the Master Direction on IT Governance, the Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls, the Cyber Security Framework, and the Master Direction on Fraud Risk Management【S2】.

The directions are issued for **commercial banks** and apply to **all banks that offer digital banking services**.  
[S4] [These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025.]  
[S1] [All banks offering digital banking services, regardless of type of facility, shall comply with the Directions contained in this chapter on a continuous basis.]

I should lodge a formal complaint against the borrower’s statutory auditor with the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) / Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) to trigger an audit of the auditor’s conduct. Pending disciplinary action by NFRA/ICAI, I must forward the complaint to the Reserve Bank (Department of Supervision, Central Office) and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) after ensuring the auditor is given an opportunity to be heard and all procedures are duly recorded. [S1]

The responsibility for reporting correct information and ensuring the accuracy of facts and figures rests with the reporting bank.  
[S1]

A commercial bank must bar additional credit to a wilful defaulter and any associated entity for **one year** after the defaulter’s name is removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters. This is stipulated in the RBI directions: “The bar on additional credit facility to the wilful defaulter or any entity with which the wilful defaulter is associated shall be effective for a period of one year after the name of wilful defaulter has been removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters by the lenders.” [S1]

A commercial bank must remove the borrower or guarantor’s name from the List of Wilful Defaulters **after the resolution plan has been implemented under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code or the RBI’s Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025**【S2】.
A commercial bank must establish a **transparent mechanism for the entire process of identifying wilful defaulters** so that penal provisions are applied fairly and without discretion. [S1]

A commercial bank must submit the information on wilful defaulters to credit information companies **at monthly intervals** [S1]. The report must contain **a list of wilful defaulters in respect of suit‑filed accounts and a list of wilful defaulters in respect of non‑suit‑filed accounts** [S1]. When a defaulter’s outstanding amount falls below ₹25 lakh (or the RBI‑notified threshold), the bank must also inform the credit information companies of the **removal of the defaulter’s name from the list** within thirty days [S1].

The bank must internally conduct a comprehensive investigation from a wilful‑default perspective before transferring the ₹30 lakh loan, and it must classify the borrower as a wilful defaulter if such default is observed and report it to credit information companies prior to transfer. A two‑stage committee is not compulsory; the investigation may be carried out without it. [S1]

A commercial bank must forward the details of such third parties to the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) for records, after satisfying itself of their involvement and giving them an opportunity to be heard, and IBA will prepare caution lists and circulate them to all regulated entities of the Reserve Bank. [S1]

Yes.  As per S1 para 10, a bank may proceed against the guarantor even without exhausting remedies against the principal debtor.  The guarantor’s liability is immediate once the bank has made a claim on them.  [S1]
Yes – the RBI may issue clarifications on how to apply the Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters Directions. The interpretation of any provision given by the RBI is final and binding. [S1]

Yes – a commercial bank must report to credit information companies the details of any guarantor who fails to honour the commitment when invoked, and such guarantors are classified as either large defaulters or wilful defaulters as the case may be. [S1]

The Directions apply to all **commercial banks** – that is, all banking companies, corresponding new banks and the State Bank of India as defined under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 – **excluding** Small Finance Banks (SFBs), Local Area Banks (LABs), Payments Banks (PBs) and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)【S4】.
The bank must require its internal auditors to specifically look into adherence to the instructions for classifying a borrower as a wilful defaulter. [S1]

A commercial bank may remove a wilful defaulter’s name from the List of Wilful Defaulters only after the borrower has fully paid the compromise amount. Until the full payment is made, the name cannot be removed even if the outstanding balance falls below ₹25 lakh or the RBI‑notified threshold. [S2]
Yes – the Directions are to be applied in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other laws, rules, regulations or directions that are currently in force. [S5]

The regulation defines a director as the director of a company that has been classified as a large defaulter or wilful defaulter and who was associated with the company at the time when the acts of omission or commission by the company or its directors led to the default. [S1]

When a CI fails to meet the prescribed timelines for updating, altering or correcting credit information, we must monitor the deviation and raise it in the periodical reports/reviews submitted to the Board/Committee of Board on customer service. [S1]

The legal backing is the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005 and the Rules and Regulations issued by the Reserve Bank of India under that Act, which require banks to report their share of loan accounts to credit information companies. [S5]
A commercial bank must review its Data Quality Index half‑yearly across all reporting segments. [S1]

A commercial bank should include suitable provisions in its loan policies and credit‑appraisal processes for obtaining Credit Information Reports (CIRs) from one or more Credit Information Companies (CICs) so that credit decisions are based on credit information available in the system. [S1]
The RBI Credit Information Reporting Directions define “Company” as a company defined under section 3 of the Companies Act, 1956 or the corresponding section under the Companies Act, 2013. [S1]
We must use **Form 2: Uniform Credit Reporting Format (Commercial)** to report credit information for the commercial segment. [S1]

The convenor of the Standing Sub‑Group must circulate the meeting agenda and notes at least fifteen (15) days before the scheduled meeting. This requirement follows from the rule for the TWG convenor, which also serves as the sub‑group convenor for that year [S1] and [S5].

The minimum SHG group loan amount that triggers a commercial bank’s obligation to collect and report credit information on individual SHG members to credit information companies is ₹1,00,000. This threshold is specified in the commercial bank guidance: “The collection and reporting of credit information in respect of SHG members will be restricted to the members of those SHGs that take loans exceeding ₹1,00,000/-. ” [S1]

The Technical Working Group (TWG) must hold meetings at least once in a calendar year. [S2]

The RBI Technical Working Group (TWG) for credit information reporting is composed of representatives from a broad range of lenders, including Public‑Sector Banks, Private‑Sector Banks, Foreign Banks, Primary (Urban) Cooperative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, All‑India Notified Financial Institutions, Non‑Banking Financial Companies, Housing Finance Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, Small‑Finance Banks and Urban Cooperative Banks【S1】【S4】.  Industry bodies represented on the TWG include the India Banks’ Association, the Micro‑Finance Institutions Network, Sa‑Dhan, Credit Information Companies (CICs) and Self‑Regulating Organizations【S1】【S4】.

If a term is not defined in the RBI Credit Information Reporting Directions, a commercial bank should refer first to the Credit Information Companies Rules, 2006 (CIC Rules) and the CIC Regulations, and if still undefined, consult the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, or the Companies Act, 2013 for the term’s meaning. [S5]

No. The directions apply only to “Commercial Banks”, which are defined as banking companies **other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks**【S2】. Therefore small finance banks, payment banks, and local area banks are excluded from the coverage of the RBI Commercial Banks – Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025【S3】.

A commercial bank must appoint a dedicated nodal point/official of contact for CICs to handle customer grievances, furnish that official’s details (email ID and telephone/mobile number) to the CICs, and notify the CICs of any changes to the nodal point/official within five calendar days of such change. [S1]

For a public sector bank, the Nomination and Remuneration Committee may be constituted only by non‑executive directors (NEDs). The Government of India nominee director and the director nominated under Section 19(f) of the SBI Act / Section 9(3)(c) of the Banking Companies Act are excluded, and the Chair of the Board cannot chair the committee. At least half of the members attending a meeting must be independent directors, one of whom must be a member of the RMCB. [S1]
The bank must finance only technically feasible, financially viable and bankable infrastructure projects, and it must not use term loans to substitute budgetary resources for those projects. [S5]

The RBI directions state that a public sector bank’s Board must fulfil four major roles: (i) overseeing the risk profile of the PSB, (ii) monitoring the integrity of its business and control mechanisms, (iii) ensuring expert management, and (iv) maximising the interests of its stakeholders【S1】.

A commercial bank must obtain regulatory approval for any additional roles or responsibilities of its MD & CEO or CEO through the Pravaah Portal (https://pravaah.rbi.org.in) as per Section 10B(8) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. [S1]

Therefore, as a compliance officer you should refuse to arrange the sanction and remind the NED of this prohibition.

The Board of a Public Sector Bank must institutionalise discussions with its management on the quality of internal control systems, and it must specifically focus on creating and sustaining a culture of control. [S1]

Yes – the Chair of the Board may be a member of the Risk Management Committee only if they possess the requisite risk‑management expertise【S1】.

The external benchmark rate is defined as the reference rate that includes the RBI policy Repo Rate, the Government of India Three‑month and Six‑month Treasury Bill yields published by Financial Benchmarks India Private Ltd (FBIL), and any other benchmark market interest rate published by FBIL [S1].  Interest rates on advances must be set with reference to such a market‑determined external benchmark [S4].
The MCLR prevailing on the date of first disbursement applies to the loan, whether that first disbursement is partial or full, and remains in effect until the next reset date. [S1]

A bank may calculate its cost of funds for the internal benchmark on the basis of average cost of funds, marginal cost of funds, or any other reasonable and transparent methodology in vogue [S3]. The chosen method must be consistent, reasonable, and transparent, and it must be made available for supervisory review or scrutiny as required [S3]. If the method uses the card rate for deposits of one or more tenors, the deposits in the chosen tenor(s) must constitute the largest share of the bank’s deposit base [S3].

Negative carry on the mandatory CRR, when returns on CRR balances are nil, is calculated as:  

**Required CRR × (marginal cost) ÷ (1 – CRR)**, using the marginal cost of funds as determined in paragraph 17. [S1]
Yes. A public sector bank may entrust the Chief Vigilance Officer with portfolios such as Inspection and Audit, Accounts, Planning and Development, and Legal matters. [S1]

No – the Directions are meant to guide banks rather than supersede existing law.  They state that banks “shall be guided by the extant regulations under Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Governance) Directions, 2025 (updated from time to time)”【S2】.
The interest rate on advances linked to an external benchmark must be reset at least once every three months. [S1]
A commercial bank must review its Base Rate at least once in a quarter, with the approval of the Board or the Asset Liability Management Committees (ALCOs) as per the bank’s practice. [S1]

The Directions allow a bank to raise the credit‑risk premium on an existing borrower only when the customer’s credit‑risk profile has deteriorated, and such a change must be supported by a full risk‑profile review [S1] [S2]. This provision does not apply to loans under consortium or multiple banking arrangements.

No. The RBI’s KYC customer‑acceptance policy for NBFCs explicitly states that the policy “shall not result in denial of a financial facility to members of the general public, especially those who are financially or socially disadvantaged, including the Persons with Disabilities (PwDs)” and that an NBFC “shall not reject an application for onboarding or periodic updation of KYC without application of mind” [S1].
The NBFC must register the details of the non‑profit customer on the DARPAN Portal of NITI Aayog. [S1]

For a partnership firm opening an account with an NBFC, you must collect the following certified copies (or equivalent e‑documents): the registration certificate, partnership deed, PAN of the partnership firm, documents as specified in paragraph 23 relating to beneficial owners, managers, officers or employees holding an attorney, the names of all partners, and the address of the registered office and principal place of business if it differs from the registered office [S1].
An NBFC must verify the UNSCR 1718 sanctions list **every day** to account for any modifications. [S1]

A loan is treated as a commercial‑real‑estate (CRE) exposure if it is to a builder, developer or other for an office building, retail space, multi‑purpose commercial premises, multitenant commercial premises, industrial or warehouse space, hotel, land acquisition, development or construction, or if it is to an individual for a third dwelling unit onwards, where repayment prospects depend mainly on lease/rental or sale cash flows. This definition is set out in the RBI guidelines for NBFCs【S2】.
